title: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
gist: After ULA's Vulcan failure destroyed 40 Amazon Leo satellites and grounded Amazon's primary launcher, Amazon is leaning on Ariane 6 (36 satellites launched, fleet now 432) and accelerating Falcon 9 flights from rival SpaceX, whose shift of Starlink to Starship frees Falcon 9 capacity, while Ariane 6 production limits and New Glenn's grounding constrain alternatives.

insights.claim: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan failure on November 15, 2026 destroyed 40 Amazon Leo satellites and grounded Vulcan, Amazon's primary launch provider, for months.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Amazon Leo deployment schedule risk rises; ULA's reliability and cadence credibility take a hit.

insights.claim: Amazon paid ULA hundreds of millions of dollars to expand Cape Canaveral facilities for up to 25 Vulcan launches per year, yet Vulcan has flown only five times (one failure) in three years.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Large sunk investment in an underperforming launcher; ULA cadence ramp is far off.

insights.claim: Amazon booked 108 launches across every available Western medium/heavy rocket to deploy 3,232 Amazon Leo satellites, but has completed only 17 flights with one failure, as most contracts relied on rockets still in development.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Constellation buildout is well behind plan, keeping Starlink's lead intact.

insights.claim: Blue Origin's New Glenn has been grounded since May 2026 after a launch-pad explosion and may resume early 2027, but Amazon slots could be hard to get as Blue Origin prioritizes NASA's Artemis work.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Bezos-linked launcher offers little near-term relief to Amazon Leo.
insights.locator: Blue Origin, owned by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

insights.claim: Amazon is accelerating Falcon 9 launches from rival SpaceX, pulling the next Amazon Leo Falcon 9 flight forward to December 2026 with several more in rapid succession.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: SpaceX profits from its main broadband competitor's dependence; Amazon Leo deployment hinges on SpaceX.
insights.locator: The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo

insights.claim: SpaceX moving Starlink launches from Falcon 9 to Starship frees Falcon 9 capacity for customers like Amazon, but SpaceX reportedly stopped accepting commercial Falcon 9 bookings after 2028.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Amazon has a closing window on its most reliable launcher; post-2028 launch supply depends on Vulcan, Ariane 6 and New Glenn maturing.
insights.locator: Starlink’s move to Starship opens up

insights.claim: Starship's ability to launch heavier, more powerful Starlink satellites will widen SpaceX's lead over Amazon and other satellite-internet competitors; Starlink already has more than 11,000 satellites.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Competitive gap in satellite broadband likely widens, favoring SpaceX valuation over Amazon Leo.

insights.claim: Amazon has hundreds of Amazon Leo satellites in storage awaiting launch, and Falcon 9 can fly from Cape Canaveral every few days, making SpaceX Amazon's most assured ride to orbit.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Launch, not satellite production, is Amazon Leo's binding constraint.
insights.locator: In the meantime, SpaceX will offer

insights.claim: Federal regulators approved Amazon Leo's second-generation constellation, which would bring the fleet to more than 7,000 satellites in the 2030s, and Amazon also plans a direct-to-device service.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Amazon's long-run ambitions require far more launch capacity than currently available.
insights.locator: The relationship between Amazon and SpaceX

insights.claim: Ariane 6 launched 36 Amazon Leo satellites, bringing the fleet to 432, and has flown four successful Amazon missions in 2026, prompting Amazon to reserve six more Arianespace flights in September.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Arianespace gains commercial credibility and backlog from Amazon.

insights.claim: Europe's rocket factories are sized for at most nine or 10 expendable Ariane 6 flights per year, and Arianespace will likely reach only six in 2026, limiting how much it can absorb Amazon's demand.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Ariane 6 cannot fill the Vulcan gap quickly; watch the European ministerial decision on a production ramp.
insights.locator: But there are questions about Europe’s ability

insights.claim: European taxpayers subsidize every Ariane 6 flight, including commercial launches for American corporations like Amazon, and ministers may decide next month on increasing Ariane 6 production.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A production-ramp decision would be a positive signal for European launch suppliers.
